title: Wealth Taxes Could Kill Privately-Owned Companies
gist: Using In-N-Out Burger owner Lynsi Snyder and California's Proposition 40 as a case study, the article argues that wealth taxes on illiquid private-company equity don't just redistribute money — they mechanically force founders to sell control, and precedent like eBay v. Newmark means even a small forced sale can legally convert a mission-driven company into a shareholder-value-maximizing one, raising an unresolved Takings Clause question.

insights.claim: California's Proposition 40, on the November 2026 ballot, would impose a one-time tax of up to 5% on the wealth of the state's billionaire residents, explicitly targeting founders whose net worth is concentrated in illiquid private-company equity.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: A live template for state-level wealth taxes on illiquid founder equity that could spread to other high-tax states with large concentrations of unicorn founders.
insights.locator: This November, California will vote on Proposition 40

insights.claim: In-N-Out Burger owner Lynsi Snyder relocated her family and established a second corporate headquarters in Tennessee last July, three months before the Prop 40 initiative was even filed with the California Attorney General — a pattern of founders pre-emptively exiting states before wealth-tax proposals formalize.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Watch for accelerating HQ/domicile relocation by concentrated private-company owners out of California ahead of the Prop 40 vote, regardless of outcome.
insights.quote: there’s a lot of great things about California, but raising a family is not easy here.
insights.locator: Then, last July, Lynsi Snyder announced

insights.claim: Proposition 40 instructs California to value any voting or controlling equity interest at no less than the holder's percentage of total voting control multiplied by the entire company's market capitalization, overriding standard appraisal practice of valuing economic ownership independently of control rights.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: This valuation formula mechanically inflates the taxable value of founder control stakes beyond a standard minority-discount appraisal, forcing larger forced share sales and greater control dilution than the statutory rate implies.
insights.quote: the percentage of the business entity owned by the taxpayer shall be presumed to be not less than the taxpayer’s percentage of the overall voting or other direct control rights.
insights.locator: The proposition's valuation rules state clearly

insights.claim: A small minority-stake transaction — such as outside investors buying 1% of a company at a $10 billion valuation — does not predict the price at which a much larger control block (e.g., a 50% founder stake) could actually be sold, because large blocks face transfer restrictions, rights of first refusal, board approval requirements, and a thin pool of buyers willing to write nine-figure checks.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Any wealth-tax regime that marks illiquid founder equity to the last small private transaction systematically overstates realizable liquidation value, understating the true tax burden on control.
insights.locator: There is no button Alice can press to sell

insights.claim: Because forced sales of large private-company blocks realize prices below the headline minority-transaction valuation, a founder must liquidate more equity than the nominal tax bill implies to raise the cash — pushing many founders below the ownership threshold needed to retain legal control of the company they built.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: The effective cost of an illiquid-wealth tax is not the statutory rate but a control-adjusted rate that can be materially higher — a structural risk for any founder-controlled company subject to such a tax.
insights.locator: To meet her tax liability, Alice has to liquidate

insights.claim: Wealth held by founders functions less like deferred consumption (mansions, jets, vacations) and more like a governance tool — the ability to keep employees and capital organized around a specific mission — so a wealth tax that forces equity sales doesn't just redistribute consumption, it strips founders of the capacity to direct their institutions.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Reframes wealth-tax debates for investors in founder-controlled companies: the real economic loss from forced dilution is optionality and mission-continuity, not just headline net worth.
insights.quote: A founder accumulates wealth precisely because he or she does not want to consume the underlying resources.

insights.claim: In-N-Out's ability to refuse franchising, keep a four-item menu, and pay associates above competitor wages is a direct function of Lynsi Snyder's sole, unchallenged ownership; a Prop-40-forced sale of even 5% of her stake would introduce the first outside shareholder and start converting the company's mandate from mission-driven to shareholder-value-driven.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Mission-driven, non-profit-maximizing private businesses are structurally more vulnerable to wealth-tax-induced ownership dilution than conventional profit-maximizing firms.

themes.theme: eBay v. Newmark as Legal Trigger

insights.claim: In eBay v. Newmark, the Delaware Court of Chancery ruled that once a for-profit Delaware corporation has outside stockholders, its controlling founders cannot justify governance decisions purely on preserving a non-monetary company culture — they are bound by fiduciary duties to maximize stockholder value for all shareholders.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Establishes the legal mechanism by which any forced minority sale (e.g., from a wealth tax) can trigger a binding shift in a private company's fiduciary obligations toward profit maximization, not just a change in cap table.
insights.quote: Having chosen a for-profit corporate form, the Craigslist directors are bound by the fiduciary duties and standards that accompany that form.

insights.claim: Under the eBay v. Newmark precedent, a founder's sovereignty over a company's non-financial mission is legally compromised the moment a single outside shareholder exists — not only once majority control (e.g., 50%) is lost — meaning a wealth tax's first forced share sale, however small, can trigger the shift toward shareholder-value governance.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating founder-controlled companies facing wealth-tax exposure should treat the first forced outside sale, not the loss of majority control, as the inflection point for governance and strategy risk.
insights.quote: Even though her control is lost at 50%, her sovereignty over the business is lost with the first outside investor.

insights.claim: After eBay bought a minority stake in Craigslist from a departing shareholder, founders Craig Newmark and Jim Buckmaster tried to adopt a poison-pill 'Rights Plan' to permanently block eBay from acquiring more of the company and preserve Craigslist's non-monetized culture — the Delaware court rejected this defense as invalid once outside stockholders existed.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Standard anti-takeover governance tools (poison pills) cannot shield a founder's non-financial mission once a company has outside shareholders — a limit relevant to any founder weighing defensive structures ahead of a forced wealth-tax sale.
insights.locator: eBay ended up launching a competitor to Craigslist

insights.claim: A hypothetical wartime scenario — a 100% tax on tungsten-inflated farmland value — functionally forces the same surrender of property as outright government condemnation, while a 50% tax still forces a sale, a 10% tax may only require borrowing, and a 5% tax (roughly Prop 40's level) sits in the ambiguous zone between ordinary taxation and de facto confiscation.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Even Prop 40's comparatively modest 5% rate cannot be assumed 'clearly just a tax' — it sits in a legally contested zone that could support a Takings Clause challenge if enacted.
insights.locator: Now imagine the tax is not 100%

insights.claim: The Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause (extended to states via the Fourteenth Amendment) already protects personal property (Horne v. Department of Agriculture), intangible business assets (Ruckelshaus v. Monsanto), ongoing-concern business value (Kimball Laundry Co. v. United States), and contractual rights (Louisville Joint Stock Land Bank v. Radford) — the author predicts Prop 40's voting-control valuation clause will force courts to decide for the first time whether control itself is a constitutionally protected property interest.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
entities: Kimball Laundry Co. v. United States
Louisville Joint Stock Land Bank v. Radford
insights.so_what: A future legal challenge to Prop 40 (or similar wealth taxes) on Takings Clause grounds is a live tail scenario worth tracking for any founder-heavy portfolio in wealth-tax states.
insights.quote: nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation.

insights.claim: Congressman Ro Khanna has endorsed a federal wealth tax proposal with a 2% annual levy on all wealth above $50 million — a threshold far below the billionaire framing of Prop 40 that would sweep in a much broader set of family businesses and founders nationally, not just tech and AI billionaires.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: A federal wealth tax at this threshold would be a much larger structural risk to private/family business ownership than any single state measure — worth monitoring as a policy tail risk beyond California.

insights.claim: The article's closing thesis is that private companies are the practical infrastructure through which Americans exercise constitutional freedoms like speech and association, so a wealth tax that forces founder-controlled firms into diffusely-held, shareholder-maximizing entities amounts to a monetary mechanism for narrowing private agency and independent institutional pluralism in the economy.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Frames wealth-tax policy risk as a structural threat to the population of mission-driven, founder-controlled private companies — worth tracking as a distinct category facing forced homogenization into conventional shareholder-value firms.

insights.claim: The author draws an analogy between constitutional rights and their private-company vehicles: free speech is a legal right, but owning a media company (or, per the George Lucas/Lucasfilm example, a film studio) is what gives someone the material capacity to actually exercise it at scale — implying that concentrated private ownership is itself a form of infrastructure for civil liberties, not merely an economic privilege.
insights.speaker: Christian Angelopoulos
insights.so_what: Investors and policymakers should weigh wealth-tax design against its effect on the diversity of independently-controlled institutions (media, tech, mission-driven firms), not only its revenue and equity effects.
insights.locator: Freedom of speech gives an individual the right to publish
